claims.text: Adding 1–3 at.% boron to phosphorus-containing CoCrFeMnNi will enhance its glass-forming ability.
Adding 1–3 at.% boron will improve the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous alloy.
The baseline phosphorus-doped CoCrFeMnNi alloy has chemical and topological order that limits glass-forming ability.
The baseline alloy's chemical and topological order limits the thermal stability of its amorphous state.
Boron addition increases atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Boron forms localized boron–metal bonds in the alloy.
The proposed short-range ordering and boron–metal bonding elevate chemical and topological disorder.
Boron forms directional bonds that disrupt long-range crystalline order.
The increased local disorder retards crystallization nucleation.
Retarded crystallization nucleation facilitates glass formation.
Retarded crystallization nucleation increases the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The boron-containing alloy will have a higher glass-transition temperature than the phosphorus-only baseline.
The boron-containing alloy will have a higher crystallization temperature than the phosphorus-only baseline.
The boron-containing alloy will have a higher critical cooling rate required for glass formation than the phosphorus-only baseline.
The beneficial effects occur only at 1–3 at.% boron.
Boron contents above 3 at.% may cause boride phase segregation.
Boride phase segregation may compromise glass-forming ability and amorphous-state thermal stability.
Using identical processing conditions and an approximately 10^6 K/s cooling rate provides a controlled comparison between baseline and boron-modified samples.

contradictions.description: Enhanced glass-forming ability conventionally corresponds to a lower critical cooling rate required to avoid crystallization, whereas the hypothesis predicts and treats an increase in the required critical cooling rate as improvement.
